hero.title: Basic Accounting and Bookkeeping: learn by doing
hero.subtitle: Learn double entry with interactive journal and equation practice, then build ledgers, trial balances, bank reconciliations and final accounts in a working spreadsheet.
hero.outcomeLine: After this course you can keep a small business's books and prepare its income statement and balance sheet.

assessment: Finish the required labs in each module: they are checked automatically and explained when something is missing.
Pass each module quiz (70% or more). You can retry as often as you like.
Complete the final accounts project and the final assessment.

faq.q: Do I need to know maths?
faq.a: Only arithmetic and percentages. Accounting is mostly careful, orderly thinking.
The examples use rupees, but double entry is the same worldwide. Local tax and legal rules are not covered.

faq.q: Will it make me an accountant?
faq.a: It gives you the foundation for bookkeeping and for professional study. Professional qualifications need further courses and exams.

activities.title: Check the accounting equation
activities.objective: Total assets and liabilities, find the owner's capital and prove the equation balances.
activities.scenario: Sana starts a small tailoring shop. List what she owns and owes, and find her capital.
steps: In B5 total the assets (B2:B4).
In B9 total the liabilities (B7:B8).
In B10 find the capital: assets minus liabilities.
In B11 show Balanced if assets equal liabilities plus capital.

checks.label: B5 is total assets
checks.explain: Assets are what the business owns.

checks.label: B9 is total liabilities
checks.explain: Liabilities are what the business owes.

checks.label: B10 is the capital
checks.explain: Capital is what is left for the owner: assets minus liabilities.

checks.label: B11 shows Balanced
checks.explain: The accounting equation says assets always equal liabilities plus capital.

activities.title: Complete a trial balance
activities.objective: Total the debit and credit columns and check that they agree.
activities.scenario: At the end of the month the ledger balances are listed. Prove that the books balance.
steps: In B11 total the Debit column.
In C11 total the Credit column.
In B12 show Agree if the totals are equal, otherwise Differ.
In B13 find the difference between the two totals (use ABS).

checks.label: B11 totals the debits
checks.explain: Debit balances are assets and expenses.

checks.label: C11 totals the credits
checks.explain: Credit balances are liabilities, capital and income.

checks.label: B12 shows Agree
checks.explain: In double entry every debit has an equal credit, so the totals must agree.

checks.label: B13 is the difference
checks.explain: A balanced trial balance has a difference of zero.

activities.title: Find the difference
activities.objective: Measure a trial balance difference and say which side is larger.
activities.scenario: A trial balance does not agree. Find the size of the difference and which side is too big, to guide the search for the mistake.
steps: Total the Debit column in B9 and the Credit column in C9.
In B10 find the difference with ABS.
In B11 show Debit side or Credit side, whichever total is larger.

checks.label: B9 totals the debits
checks.explain: Add every debit balance.

checks.label: C9 totals the credits
checks.explain: Add every credit balance.

checks.label: B10 is the difference
checks.explain: The difference tells you how big the error is.

checks.label: B11 says which side is larger
checks.explain: A larger debit side suggests a debit was overstated or a credit left out.

activities.title: Balance a cash account
activities.objective: Total both sides of a ledger account and find its balance.
activities.scenario: Here is the cash account for the month. Receipts are on the debit side and payments on the credit side. Find the balance carried down.
steps: In B8 total the debit side (B2:B4).
In D8 total the credit side (D2:D5).
In B10 find the balance: debit total minus credit total.
In B11 show Debit balance or Credit balance with IF.

checks.label: B8 totals the debit side
checks.explain: Add the receipts.

checks.label: D8 totals the credit side
checks.explain: Add the payments.

checks.label: B10 is the balance
checks.explain: The balance is the difference between the two sides.

checks.label: B11 says Debit balance
checks.explain: A positive result means more came in than went out: cash in hand.

activities.title: Write up a cash book
activities.objective: Record receipts and payments and find the closing balance.
activities.scenario: A stall owner keeps a cash book for a week. Find the total received, the total paid and the cash left.
steps: In B9 total the receipts (B3:B8).
In D9 total the payments (D3:D7).
In B11 find the closing balance: opening balance plus receipts minus payments.
In B12 check it with IF: show Low if the closing balance is under 5,000, otherwise OK.

checks.label: B9 totals the receipts
checks.explain: Add every receipt.

checks.label: D9 totals the payments
checks.explain: Add every payment.

checks.label: B11 is the closing balance
checks.explain: Opening balance plus receipts minus payments.

checks.label: B12 says OK
checks.explain: A simple check helps spot a cash shortage early.

activities.title: Reconcile the bank balance
activities.objective: Explain the difference between the cash book and the bank statement.
activities.scenario: The cash book shows 24,500 but the bank statement shows 27,800. Two timing differences explain it.
steps: In B6 work out the adjusted bank balance: statement balance, minus unpresented cheques, plus uncredited deposits.
In B7 find the difference between the adjusted bank balance and the cash book balance.
In B8 show Reconciled if the difference is zero, otherwise Investigate.

checks.label: B6 is the adjusted bank balance
checks.explain: Cheques not yet cashed still leave the account; deposits not yet shown will arrive.

checks.label: B7 is the difference
checks.explain: After adjustments the two balances should agree.

checks.label: B8 says Reconciled
checks.explain: A zero difference means the timing differences explain everything.

cells.A4: Uncredited deposits (paid in, not yet shown)

activities.title: A straight-line depreciation schedule
activities.objective: Spread the cost of an asset over its useful life and track its book value.
activities.scenario: A machine costs 1,20,000, will last five years and then be worth 20,000. Build the yearly schedule.
steps: In B4 work out the yearly depreciation: (cost minus scrap value) divided by the life.
In B8 write year 1's depreciation (the locked yearly amount) and in C8 the accumulated depreciation; in D8 the book value (cost minus accumulated).
Copy the pattern down to year 5.

checks.label: B4 is the yearly depreciation
checks.explain: Straight line spreads the depreciable amount evenly.

checks.label: D8 is the book value after year 1
checks.explain: Book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation.

checks.label: C10 is the accumulated depreciation after year 3
checks.explain: Each year's depreciation is added to the running total.

checks.label: D12 equals the scrap value after year 5
checks.hint: Fill the pattern down to row 12.
checks.explain: By the end of its life the asset is worth only its scrap value.

activities.title: Prepare an income statement
activities.objective: Work out cost of goods sold, gross profit and net profit, and the margins.
activities.scenario: A shop's year-end figures are below. Prepare its income statement.
steps: In B8 find the cost of goods sold: opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock.
In B9 find the gross profit: sales minus cost of goods sold.
In B14 total the expenses (B10:B13) and in B15 find the net profit.
In B16 find the gross profit margin (gross profit divided by sales) and in B17 the net profit margin.

checks.label: B8 is the cost of goods sold
checks.explain: Opening stock plus purchases less what is left.

checks.label: B9 is the gross profit
checks.explain: Sales minus the cost of the goods sold.

checks.label: B14 totals the expenses
checks.explain: Add every running expense.

checks.label: B15 is the net profit
checks.explain: Gross profit less expenses.

checks.label: B16 is the gross profit margin
checks.explain: Margins let you compare businesses of different sizes.

checks.label: B17 is the net profit margin
checks.explain: Net profit as a share of sales.

activities.title: Final project: from figures to final accounts
activities.objective: Prepare an income statement and prove the balance sheet balances.
activities.scenario: Use the year-end figures to find net profit, closing capital, total assets and total liabilities, and show that the books balance.
steps: In B16 find the cost of goods sold (opening stock + purchases - closing stock).
In B17 find the gross profit and in B18 the total expenses (rent, wages, other).
In B19 find the net profit and in B20 the closing capital (opening capital + net profit - drawings).
In B21 total the assets (cash, debtors, closing stock, equipment) and in B22 the liabilities (creditors, loan).
In B23 show Balanced if assets equal closing capital plus liabilities.

checks.label: B16 is the cost of goods sold
checks.explain: Opening stock plus purchases less closing stock.

checks.label: B17 is the gross profit
checks.explain: Sales less cost of goods sold.

checks.label: B18 totals the expenses
checks.explain: Rent, wages and other expenses.

checks.label: B19 is the net profit
checks.explain: Gross profit less expenses.

checks.label: B20 is the closing capital
checks.explain: Opening capital plus profit less drawings.

checks.label: B21 totals the assets
checks.explain: Cash, debtors, closing stock and equipment.

checks.label: B22 totals the liabilities
checks.explain: Creditors and the bank loan.

checks.label: B23 shows Balanced
checks.explain: Assets equal capital plus liabilities when the books are right.
